newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire gorilla park revives after refugees move out.
newsitem.headline: Zaire gorilla park revives after refugees move out.

text.p: Mountain gorillas and other rare animals in an eastern Zaire park are enjoying a break from poaching and habitat destruction with the departure of Zairean soldiers and hundreds of thousands of Rwandan refugees, conservationists say.

"Cautiously, I would say that prospects for the park are looking better than they have for a long time," Popol Verhoestraete, a representative of the International Gorilla Conservation Programme (IGCP), told Reuters at the weekend.

Areas around the Virunga National Park, founded in 1925 and the oldest in Africa, are now occupied by rebels of the Alliance of Democratic Forces who put to flight the Zaire army and over 700,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees whose camps abutted the park.
Made famous by American naturalist Dian Fossey and the film "Gorillas in the Mist", the park's star attraction, its mountain gorillas, live only in Virunga and nearby forests in Rwanda and Uganda.

During the two and a half years they lived near the camp, the Rwandans destroyed an estimated 45 square km (17 square miles) of forest and damaged at least 160 square km (64 square miles), park workers said.

Daily harvesting firewood and building materials, they had begun to work their way up the slopes of still-active volcanoes towards the 125 square km (48 square mile) refuge of an estimated 350 mountain gorillas.
But most of the Hutu refugees, who fled Rwanda in 1994 after the genocide of hundreds of thousands of Tutsis, returned home in November as the Alliance rebels took over.
The rebels, fighting to topple Zaire president Mobutu Sese Seko, have promised to do their best to preserve the park. They say tourists could provide a source of revenue to the new authorities.
"At first the local people thought that if they had been liberated by the rebels it meant they had been liberated from obeying park rules about farming and killing animals," said Verhoestraete.
"But the new governor of the area understands the benefits of conservation and is doing what he can to protect the park."
Killing the animals is banned and rebel soldiers can confiscate any vehicle found to be carrying meat from the park's animals.
At least for the moment, the herds of buffalo and antelope that graze plains 100 km (65 miles) north of Goma are not being hunted on the almost industrial scale see with Zairean soldiers.
Not hard to miss with an automatic assault rifle, the hippopotamus population has been literally decimated and is now estimated at little more than 2,000 -- from 20,000 before.

The hippos -- lumbering lumps of meat that lived at a greater density in the park than anywhere else in the world -- were a valuable source of income for Zairean soldiers who also forced refugees to carry meat for their hunting parties.
Gorillas, too, were victims of poaching or were accidentally caught in traps -- at least four were killed in 1995.
With the refugees gone, the park's authorities now face the prospect of trying to repair the damage to the park, without the tourists whose visits to the gorillas were the main source of income.
"With the gorillas we have here that are already habituated we could be earning at least $48,000 a month, which is a significant amount for the park," said Verhoestraete.
"If all goes well then, tourist visits could be possible in the early months of this year, and certainly by the end."
